warmup.q: In Java, Integer a = 127, b = 127; and Integer c = 128, d = 128;. What do a == b and c == d print with default JVM settings?
options: It doesn't compile: == can't compare Integer objects
warmup.why: Autoboxing calls Integer.valueOf, which always returns a cached, shared instance for -128 to 127. So a and b are the same object. 128 is outside the cache, so c and d are two different objects with equal values, and == compares references. That shared cache is a flyweight, and it's the reason boxed == bugs pass tests with small numbers.

sections.h: Composite: a tree you price like a single rule
sections.html:
A merchant's fee plan is rarely one number. It's 0.30 plus 2.9%, plus a bundle of add-ons, and the bundle has rules of its own. Composite lets a group of rules and a single rule share one interface. A group answers by asking each of its children, so the code that prices a payment never checks whether it holds a leaf or a whole tree.

The GoF version is an abstract Component class with add and remove methods that leaves must implement somehow. Java 21 and Kotlin replace it with a sealed type and one exhaustive switch:

Java
sealed interface Rule permits Flat, Percent, AllOf {}
record Flat(long minor) implements Rule {}
record Percent(int bps) implements Rule {}
record AllOf(List<Rule> rules) implements Rule {
    AllOf { rules = List.copyOf(rules); }            // immutable: copy what the caller passed
}

static long fee(Rule r, long amountMinor) {
    return switch (r) {                               // no default
        case Flat f -> f.minor();
        case Percent p -> amountMinor * p.bps() / 10_000;
        case AllOf a -> a.rules().stream().mapToLong(x -> fee(x, amountMinor)).sum();
    };
}

Rule plan = new AllOf(List.of(new Flat(30), new Percent(290), new AllOf(List.of(new Flat(5)))));
Kotlin
sealed interface Rule {
    data class Flat(val minor: Long) : Rule
    data class Percent(val bps: Int) : Rule
    class AllOf(rules: List<Rule>) : Rule {
        val rules: List<Rule> = rules.toList()         // immutable: copy what the caller passed
    }
}

fun fee(r: Rule, amountMinor: Long): Long = when (r) {   // no else
    is Rule.Flat -> r.minor
    is Rule.Percent -> amountMinor * r.bps / 10_000
    is Rule.AllOf -> r.rules.sumOf { fee(it, amountMinor) }
}

val plan = Rule.AllOf(listOf(Rule.Flat(30), Rule.Percent(290), Rule.AllOf(listOf(Rule.Flat(5)))))

For a 100.00 payment, fee(plan, 10_000) is 30 + 290 + 5 = 325. The recursion follows the tree: AllOf adds up whatever its children return, and the children don't care who asked.

The sealed type buys you two things. The switch has no default, so adding a Capped node makes javac report "the switch expression does not cover all possible input values" (kotlinc: "'when' expression must be exhaustive") at every place that prices or prints a plan. And a second operation over the same tree, such as describe, is just another function. The node classes don't change.

Keep the tree immutable. List.copyOf in the compact constructor copies the caller's list, so a later edit to that list can't reach into a plan that is already in use. Kotlin's List is only a read-only view, so copy with toList(). An immutable tree can't grow a cycle, and threads can share it safely, which the last section relies on.

try.title: Price a tree, then let the caller mutate it
steps: Open CompositeDemo.java (or CompositeDemo.kt). Before you run it, work out the two fees in your head.
Run it with the command below and check your numbers. Note the last line.
Remove the copy: in Java delete the compact constructor AllOf { rules = List.copyOf(rules); }; in Kotlin change = rules.toList() to = rules. Predict the last line, then run.

code.title: CompositeDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l06; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** A fee plan as a tree. Leaves and groups share one sealed type, so one switch prices them all. */ public class CompositeDemo { sealed interface Rule permits Flat, Percent, AllOf {} record Flat(long minor) implements Rule {} record Percent(int bps) implements Rule {} record AllOf(List<Rule> rules) implements Rule { AllOf { rules = List.copyOf(rules); } // copy what we were given: the tree stays immutable } static long fee(Rule r, long amountMinor) { return switch (r) { // no default: a new node type breaks the build case Flat f -> f.minor(); case Percent p -> amountMinor * p.bps() / 10_000; case AllOf a -> a.rules().stream().mapToLong(x -> fee(x, amountMinor)).sum(); }; } static String describe(Rule r) { return switch (r) { case Flat f -> Long.toString(f.minor()); case Percent p -> String.format("%d.%02d%%", p.bps() / 100, p.bps() % 100); case AllOf a -> "(" + String.join(" + ", a.rules().stream().map(CompositeDemo::describe).toList()) + ")"; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Rule> bundle = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Flat(5))); Rule plan = new AllOf(List.of(new Flat(30), new Percent(290), new AllOf(bundle))); System.out.println("plan: " + describe(plan)); System.out.println("fee on 100.00: " + fee(plan, 10_000)); System.out.println("fee on 1,000.00: " + fee(plan, 100_000)); bundle.add(new Flat(1_000)); // someone edits the list they passed in System.out.println("after editing the source list: " + describe(plan)); } }

alt.title: CompositeDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l06 // A fee plan as a tree. Leaves and groups share one sealed type, so one `when` prices them all. sealed interface FeeRule { data class Flat(val minor: Long) : FeeRule data class Percent(val bps: Int) : FeeRule class AllOf(rules: List<FeeRule>) : FeeRule { val rules: List<FeeRule> = rules.toList() // copy what we were given: the tree stays immutable } } private fun fee(r: FeeRule, amountMinor: Long): Long = when (r) { // no else: a new node type breaks the build is FeeRule.Flat -> r.minor is FeeRule.Percent -> amountMinor * r.bps / 10_000 is FeeRule.AllOf -> r.rules.sumOf { fee(it, amountMinor) } } private fun describe(r: FeeRule): String = when (r) { is FeeRule.Flat -> r.minor.toString() is FeeRule.Percent -> "%d.%02d%%".format(r.bps / 100, r.bps % 100) is FeeRule.AllOf -> r.rules.joinToString(" + ", "(", ")") { describe(it) } } fun main() { val bundle = mutableListOf<FeeRule>(FeeRule.Flat(5)) val plan = FeeRule.AllOf(listOf(FeeRule.Flat(30), FeeRule.Percent(290), FeeRule.AllOf(bundle))) println("plan: ${describe(plan)}") println("fee on 100.00: ${fee(plan, 10_000)}") println("fee on 1,000.00: ${fee(plan, 100_000)}") bundle += FeeRule.Flat(1_000) // someone edits the list they passed in println("after editing the source list: ${describe(plan)}") }

try.expect: plan: (30 + 2.90% + (5)), fees 325 and 2935 (30 + 2,900 + 5), and after editing the source list: (30 + 2.90% + (5)). Without the copy, the last line becomes (30 + 2.90% + (5 + 1000)): a plan already in use silently gained a 10.00 fee because someone edited the list they built it from.

sections.h: Bridge: two dimensions without N times M classes
sections.html:
Payment ops wants alerts: payment failed, fraud suspected, settlement late. Each must go out by SMS, email or Slack. Model that with inheritance (PaymentFailedSms, PaymentFailedEmail and so on) and you write nine classes. A fourth channel costs three more, each a near copy of its neighbors.

Bridge splits the two dimensions. One side is the abstraction: what happened, the alert. The other is the implementor: how it travels, the channel. The alert holds a channel and calls it:

Java
interface Channel { void deliver(String to, String body); }             // implementor: how it travels

sealed interface Alert permits PaymentFailed, FraudSuspected {           // abstraction: what happened
    void raise(String to);
}
record PaymentFailed(Channel channel, String paymentId) implements Alert {
    public void raise(String to) { channel.deliver(to, "payment " + paymentId + " failed"); }
}
record FraudSuspected(Channel channel, String last4, int score) implements Alert {
    public void raise(String to) { channel.deliver(to, "card ****" + last4 + " flagged, risk " + score); }
}

new PaymentFailed(sms, "pay_881").raise("on-call");
new PaymentFailed(email, "pay_881").raise("on-call");   // same alert, other channel: no new class
Kotlin
fun interface Channel { fun deliver(to: String, body: String) }          // implementor: how it travels

sealed interface Alert { fun raise(to: String) }                           // abstraction: what happened
data class PaymentFailed(val channel: Channel, val paymentId: String) : Alert {
    override fun raise(to: String) = channel.deliver(to, "payment $paymentId failed")
}
data class FraudSuspected(val channel: Channel, val last4: String, val score: Int) : Alert {
    override fun raise(to: String) = channel.deliver(to, "card ****$last4 flagged, risk $score")
}

PaymentFailed(sms, "pay_881").raise("on-call")
PaymentFailed(email, "pay_881").raise("on-call")    // same alert, other channel: no new class

Three alert types and three channels are now six small pieces, and a new channel is one more. Every alert works with it, because alerts only know Channel. Tests pass a recording lambda as the channel and check the text, with no SMS vendor in sight.

In Kotlin the implementor side often shrinks to a function. With fun interface Channel, the lambda Channel { to, body -> slack.post(to, body) } is a whole channel. A plain function type, (String, String) -> Unit, works as well.

Bridge is easy to confuse with Adapter, because both put an interface between two pieces of code. The difference is when and why. You design a bridge up front, because you know two things will vary on their own. You write an adapter afterwards, because a class you can't change has the wrong interface. They often meet: each channel is usually an adapter around a vendor SDK, like the issuer adapter in Adapter and Facade.

Skip the bridge when only one dimension varies. If every alert goes by email, an alert with a Mailer field is plain composition, and calling it a pattern adds nothing.

try.title: Add a channel without touching an alert
steps: Run BridgeDemo in either language and count the lines: 2 alert types times 2 channels.

Add a Slack channel. Java: record Slack() implements Channel { public String deliver(String to, String body) { return "SLACK #" + to + ": " + body; } }, then add new Slack() to the list. Kotlin: private val slack = AlertChannel { to, body -> "SLACK #$to: $body" }, then add slack to the list.
Predict how many lines print and how many alert types you had to edit. Run it.

code.title: BridgeDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l06; import java.util.List; /** Alerts (what happened) and channels (how it travels) vary on their own: 2 + 2 classes, not 2 x 2. */ public class BridgeDemo { // the implementor side: how a message travels interface Channel { String deliver(String to, String body); } record Sms() implements Channel { public String deliver(String to, String body) { return "SMS to " + to + ": " + body; } } record Email() implements Channel { public String deliver(String to, String body) { return "EMAIL to " + to + ": " + body; } } // the abstraction side: what happened. Each alert HOLDS a channel instead of being one. sealed interface Alert permits PaymentFailed, FraudSuspected { Channel channel(); String raise(String to); } record PaymentFailed(Channel channel, String paymentId, String reason) implements Alert { public String raise(String to) { return channel.deliver(to, "payment " + paymentId + " failed: " + reason); } } record FraudSuspected(Channel channel, String last4, int score) implements Alert { public String raise(String to) { return channel.deliver(to, "card ****" + last4 + " flagged, risk " + score); } } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Channel> channels = List.of(new Sms(), new Email()); for (Channel ch : channels) { System.out.println(new PaymentFailed(ch, "pay_881", "issuer declined (51)").raise("on-call")); System.out.println(new FraudSuspected(ch, "4242", 91).raise("risk-team")); } } }

alt.title: BridgeDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l06 // Alerts (what happened) and channels (how it travels) vary on their own: 2 + 2 pieces, not 2 x 2. // the implementor side: one method, so a lambda is enough fun interface AlertChannel { fun deliver(to: String, body: String): String } private val sms = AlertChannel { to, body -> "SMS to $to: $body" } private val email = AlertChannel { to, body -> "EMAIL to $to: $body" } // the abstraction side: what happened. Each alert HOLDS a channel instead of being one. sealed interface PaymentAlert { val channel: AlertChannel fun raise(to: String): String data class PaymentFailed(override val channel: AlertChannel, val paymentId: String, val reason: String) : PaymentAlert { override fun raise(to: String) = channel.deliver(to, "payment $paymentId failed: $reason") } data class FraudSuspected(override val channel: AlertChannel, val last4: String, val score: Int) : PaymentAlert { override fun raise(to: String) = channel.deliver(to, "card ****$last4 flagged, risk $score") } } fun main() { val channels = listOf(sms, email) for (ch in channels) { println(PaymentAlert.PaymentFailed(ch, "pay_881", "issuer declined (51)").raise("on-call")) println(PaymentAlert.FraudSuspected(ch, "4242", 91).raise("risk-team")) } }

try.expect: Four lines before; six after, the last two starting SLACK #on-call and SLACK #risk-team. You edited zero alert types. In Kotlin the new channel was one lambda; in Java it was one small record.

sections.h: Flyweight: share immutable objects instead of building new ones
sections.html:
Run Integer a = 127, b = 127; and a == b is true. Make both 128 and it's false. Integer.valueOf, which autoboxing calls, "will always cache values in the range -128 to 127, inclusive", so small values come from a shared pool and larger ones are new objects. That cache is a flyweight: many users share one immutable instance instead of each holding a copy.

The JDK has more of them. The JVM interns string literals, keeping one String per literal, and s.intern() returns the pooled copy of any string. Currency "is designed so that there's never more than one Currency instance for any given currency", which is why it has no public constructor and you call Currency.getInstance("EUR"). Enums are flyweights by definition, and so are Kotlin's object and data object.

The cache also explains one of the oldest bugs in Java payment code:

Java
Long settled = ledger.get("EUR");        // 25_000L, boxed when it went into the map
Long expected = report.get("EUR");       // 25_000L, boxed separately
if (settled == expected) { ... }         // false: two different Long objects
if (settled.equals(expected)) { ... }    // true
Kotlin
val settled: Long? = ledger["EUR"]       // 25_000L
val expected: Long? = report["EUR"]      // 25_000L
if (settled == expected) { /* ... */ }   // true: == calls equals()
if (settled === expected) { /* ... */ }  // false, and the compiler warns

Java's == on objects compares references. With test amounts under 128 the cache makes it pass; with real amounts it fails. Kotlin's == calls equals, so you only meet this bug with ===, and on Long? kotlinc warns that "identity equality for arguments of types 'Long?' and 'Long?' is prohibited".

You build your own flyweight with a canonicalizing factory: a private constructor and an of method that returns the pooled instance from a ConcurrentHashMap. Use computeIfAbsent. It checks and inserts in one atomic step, so eight threads asking for a new code at the same moment still get one instance. A get followed by a put on a miss is check-then-act, and under load it builds duplicates.

Two more rules keep flyweights safe. They must be immutable, because every holder sees every change. And the pool must be bounded: interning merchant names from webhook payloads grows a map that never shrinks. Pool a known set, such as the merchant category codes in a reference table.

try.title: Find out which objects are shared
steps: Read FlyweightDemo.java (or FlyweightDemo.kt) and predict all five lines before you run it.
Run it with the command below.
Break the pool: make Mcc.of return new Mcc(code) (Kotlin: make MccCode.of return MccCode(code)). Predict the last line, then run.

code.title: FlyweightDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l06; import java.util.Currency; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Four flyweights: three from the JDK, one of our own. `==` asks "the same object?" */ public class FlyweightDemo { // our own: one shared instance per merchant category code static final class Mcc { private static final Map<String, Mcc> POOL = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private static final AtomicInteger BUILT = new AtomicInteger(); final String code; private Mcc(String code) { this.code = code; BUILT.incrementAndGet(); } static Mcc of(String code) { return POOL.computeIfAbsent(code, Mcc::new); } static int built() { return BUILT.get(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Integer a = 127, b = 127; Integer c = 128, d = 128; System.out.println("Integer 127 == 127: " + (a == b)); System.out.println("Integer 128 == 128: " + (c == d) + " equals: " + c.equals(d)); String parsed = new String("5411"); // a fresh object, like a field parsed from a message System.out.println("parsed == \"5411\": " + (parsed == "5411") + " after intern(): " + (parsed.intern() == "5411")); System.out.println("Currency EUR == EUR: " + (Currency.getInstance("EUR") == Currency.getInstance("EUR"))); Mcc first = Mcc.of("5411"), second = Mcc.of("5411"); System.out.println("Mcc 5411 == 5411: " + (first == second) + " instances built: " + Mcc.built()); } }

alt.title: FlyweightDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l06 import java.util.Currency import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger // Four flyweights: three from the JDK, one of our own. In Kotlin, `==` is equals(); `===` asks "the same object?" // our own: one shared instance per merchant category code class MccCode private constructor(val code: String) { init { built.incrementAndGet() } companion object { private val pool = ConcurrentHashMap<String, MccCode>() private val built = AtomicInteger() fun of(code: String): MccCode = pool.computeIfAbsent(code) { MccCode(it) } val instancesBuilt: Int get() = built.get() } } fun main() { // typed as Any so Kotlin boxes them, as Java does for Integer; === on Int? gets a compiler warning val a: Any = 127 val b: Any = 127 val c: Any = 128 val d: Any = 128 println("Integer 127 === 127: ${a === b}") println("Integer 128 === 128: ${c === d} ==: ${c == d}") val parsed = String(charArrayOf('5', '4', '1', '1')) // a fresh object, like a field parsed from a message println("parsed === \"5411\": ${parsed === "5411"} after intern(): ${parsed.intern() === "5411"}") println("Currency EUR === EUR: ${Currency.getInstance("EUR") === Currency.getInstance("EUR")}") val first = MccCode.of("5411") val second = MccCode.of("5411") println("Mcc 5411 === 5411: ${first === second} instances built: ${MccCode.instancesBuilt}") }

try.expect: 127 is shared (true), 128 is not (false, though equals is true), a parsed "5411" is a different object until you call intern(), Currency hands out one EUR, and the pool gives one Mcc with instances built: 1. Without the pool the last line reads false instances built: 2.

sections.h: Share the tree, pass in the amount
sections.html:
Composite and Flyweight work well together. A platform with 40,000 merchants rarely has 40,000 fee plans. It has a dozen: standard, high-risk, marketplace and a few negotiated ones. Build each plan tree once at startup and let every merchant point at one of them, instead of parsing a plan per merchant per payment.

The GoF book names the split that makes this work. Intrinsic state lives inside the shared object and is the same for every user: the rates and caps in the plan. Extrinsic state belongs to one use, so the caller passes it in: the payment amount. That's why fee takes the amount as an argument. A plan that kept "the current amount" in a field could not be shared, by two merchants or by two threads.

Sharing across threads costs nothing here, because the trees never change. Records have final fields, List.copyOf returns an unmodifiable list, and an object that never changes can be read by 200 request threads at once with no lock, once it has been published safely (in a static final field, or set before the threads start). Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal in the concurrency track showed why that holds.

The same thinking fits the small values on every payment: currencies, merchant categories, card networks, response codes. If the set is closed and known when you compile, an enum (Java) or enum class (Kotlin) is the flyweight, with no pool to write. Reach for a pooled factory only when the set is open but bounded, such as category codes loaded from a table.

In the lab you build both halves: a five-node pricing composite with two operations, and a merchant-category flyweight that stays correct when eight threads ask for the same code at once.

Check yourself. Merchants want to see "fees charged this month", and a teammate adds a var monthTotal to the shared root of the standard plan. What goes wrong, and where should the total live? (Every merchant on the standard plan points at that one root, so they all add to one total, and two request threads adding at once can lose an update. The total is extrinsic state: keep it per merchant, outside the tree.)

analogy: Think of a print shop. A job is either one sheet or a folder of jobs, and you price both by asking the same question: what does this cost? That's Composite. The paper stock is a flyweight: a hundred jobs say "A4, 90 g" and all point at one stock description, while each job brings its own page count, the extrinsic part. The job and the machine are a bridge: any job can go to the laser printer or the plotter. The analogy breaks on sharing. Two jobs can't print on the same physical sheet, but two payments can use the same fee plan object at the same instant, because nothing in it ever changes.
world: Merchant onboarding probably stores fee plans as JSON or as rows in Oracle. Parse each plan into an immutable sealed tree once, cache it by plan id, and the pricing path in your Quarkus authorization service becomes a pure function, fee(plan, amount), that you test with no database. Your notification service is a bridge whether or not anyone named it: alert types from Kafka topics on one side, channel adapters around the SMS and email vendors on the other. And a Kafka consumer that deserializes a million payment events an hour builds a million "EUR" strings; mapping them to Currency.getInstance and enums at the edge leaves one object per value. In Java code, compare those amounts with equals or as primitive long, never == on Long.
mistake: The most common mistake is comparing boxed numbers with == in Java: if (entity.getAmountMinor() == expected) where both are Long. It passes every unit test, because test amounts like 100 or 50 sit inside the -128 to 127 cache and come back as the same shared object. In production a 250.00 payment is 25,000 minor units, the two Longs are different objects, and the check is false. People make it because == works on long, and nothing in the code shows the boxing. Use equals or Objects.equals(a, b), or better, keep amounts as primitive long in your domain types. In Kotlin, == already calls equals; only === has the bug, and the compiler warns on it.

compare.title: A flyweight that callers can't bypass

java.title: CardBin.java
java.html: // Not a record: a record's canonical constructor can't be private, // so `new CardBin(...)` would always bypass the pool. public final class CardBin { private static final Map<String, CardBin> POOL = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private final String bin; // first six digits of the card number private final String issuer; private CardBin(String bin, String issuer) { this.bin = bin; this.issuer = issuer; } public static CardBin of(String bin, Function<String, String> issuerLookup) { return POOL.computeIfAbsent(bin, b -> new CardBin(b, issuerLookup.apply(b))); // built once per BIN } public String bin() { return bin; } public String issuer() { return issuer; } }

kotlin.title: CardBin.kt
kotlin.html: // A plain class: a private constructor holds, and there is no generated copy() to go around it. class CardBin private constructor(val bin: String, val issuer: String) { companion object { private val pool = ConcurrentHashMap<String, CardBin>() fun of(bin: String, issuerLookup: (String) -> String): CardBin = pool.computeIfAbsent(bin) { CardBin(it, issuerLookup(it)) } // built once per BIN } }

compare.note: Both use computeIfAbsent, so the lookup runs at most once per BIN even under contention. The real difference is what each language lets you hide. A Java record would be the natural value type, but javac rejects a private canonical constructor ("attempting to assign stronger access privileges; was public"), so anyone could call new and skip the pool: use a final class. In Kotlin, a data class with a private constructor still exposes a public copy() in 2.4.21 unless you add @ConsistentCopyVisibility, as Builder and Prototype showed, so a plain class is the safe choice there too. Kotlin also makes the flyweight's identity matter less: == calls equals, so the pool is about memory and one place to validate, not about making comparisons work. For a closed set, skip the pool and use an enum in either language.

worked.title: Turn an alert class explosion into a bridge

steps.say: The notification module grew by inheritance. Count the classes, then count what a WhatsApp channel would cost.
steps.code: abstract class Alert { abstract void send(); } class PaymentFailedSms extends Alert { void send() { sms.send(phone, "payment " + id + " failed"); } } class PaymentFailedEmail extends Alert { void send() { mail.send(address, "Payment alert", "payment " + id + " failed"); } } class FraudSuspectedSms extends Alert { void send() { /* the SMS code again */ } } class FraudSuspectedEmail extends Alert { void send() { /* the email code again */ } } // WhatsApp: PaymentFailedWhatsApp, FraudSuspectedWhatsApp, and one more per future alert

alt.html: abstract class Alert { abstract fun send() } class PaymentFailedSms : Alert() { override fun send() = sms.send(phone, "payment $id failed") } class PaymentFailedEmail : Alert() { override fun send() = mail.send(address, "Payment alert", "payment $id failed") } class FraudSuspectedSms : Alert() { override fun send() { /* the SMS code again */ } } class FraudSuspectedEmail : Alert() { override fun send() { /* the email code again */ } } // WhatsApp: PaymentFailedWhatsApp, FraudSuspectedWhatsApp, and one more per future alert

steps.say: Four classes for two alerts and two channels, and WhatsApp adds two more. Name the two dimensions: what happened decides the text, the channel decides the transport. Pull the transport out behind one interface, the implementor.
steps.code: interface Channel { void deliver(String to, String body); } // 1. the implementor side record SmsChannel(SmsVendor sms) implements Channel { // 2. one class per transport, public void deliver(String to, String body) { sms.send(to, body); } // usually an adapter } record EmailChannel(MailVendor mail) implements Channel { public void deliver(String to, String body) { mail.send(to, "Payment alert", body); } }

alt.html: fun interface Channel { fun deliver(to: String, body: String) } // 1. the implementor side class SmsChannel(private val sms: SmsVendor) : Channel { // 2. one class per transport, override fun deliver(to: String, body: String) = sms.send(to, body) // usually an adapter } class EmailChannel(private val mail: MailVendor) : Channel { override fun deliver(to: String, body: String) = mail.send(to, "Payment alert", body) }

steps.say: Each alert now holds a channel and builds only its text. Ask yourself: which alert type would change if the SMS vendor changed its API? None. Only SmsChannel would.
steps.code: sealed interface Alert permits PaymentFailed, FraudSuspected { void raise(String to); } // 3. the abstraction side record PaymentFailed(Channel channel, String paymentId) implements Alert { public void raise(String to) { channel.deliver(to, "payment " + paymentId + " failed"); } } record FraudSuspected(Channel channel, String last4, int score) implements Alert { public void raise(String to) { channel.deliver(to, "card ****" + last4 + " flagged, risk " + score); } }

alt.html: sealed interface Alert { fun raise(to: String) } // 3. the abstraction side data class PaymentFailed(val channel: Channel, val paymentId: String) : Alert { override fun raise(to: String) = channel.deliver(to, "payment $paymentId failed") } data class FraudSuspected(val channel: Channel, val last4: String, val score: Int) : Alert { override fun raise(to: String) = channel.deliver(to, "card ****$last4 flagged, risk $score") }

steps.say: Test each side alone. A recording lambda is a complete channel, so alert tests need no vendor at all. WhatsApp is now one class, and no alert changes.
steps.code: List<String> sent = new ArrayList<>(); Channel recording = (to, body) -> sent.add(to + ": " + body); // 4. a fake channel in one line new PaymentFailed(recording, "pay_881").raise("on-call"); assertThat(sent).containsExactly("on-call: payment pay_881 failed");

alt.html: val sent = mutableListOf<String>() val recording = Channel { to, body -> sent += "$to: $body" } // 4. a fake channel in one line PaymentFailed(recording, "pay_881").raise("on-call") assertThat(sent).containsExactly("on-call: payment pay_881 failed")

lab.title: A pricing composite and a merchant-category flyweight
steps: Read the five node types in PricingRule.kt; they are given. Run the tests: all eight fail.
Write fee as one when (this) with five branches and no else. Leaves compute; AllOf sums its children, CheapestOf takes their minimum, Capped takes minOf(rule.fee(amountMinor), capMinor).
Write describe the same way, following the formats in its KDoc.
In MerchantCategory, add a private pool to the companion object and write of: reject unknown codes first, then return the pooled instance.
Run the tests until all eight pass. Then add data class Discount(val bps: Int) : PricingRule to the sealed interface, read the two compiler errors, and delete it again.
hints: rules.sumOf { it.fee(amountMinor) } returns a Long when the lambda does, and an empty list sums to 0. rules.minOf { ... } works the same way for CheapestOf.
joinToString(" + ", "(", ")") { it.describe() } takes a separator, a prefix and a postfix, and gives () for an empty list. "%d.%02d%%".format(bps / 100, bps % 100) turns 5 into 0.05%.

requireNotNull(KNOWN[code]) { "unknown MCC: $code" } throws IllegalArgumentException. Then pool.computeIfAbsent(code) { MerchantCategory(it, description) }: a get then put would let two threads both build one.

drill.title: The pricing composite from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a sealed Rule with Flat, Percent and an immutable AllOf, and a fee function that prices any tree with one exhaustive switch (or when) and no default. Then price AllOf(Flat(30), Percent(290)) on 10,000 in your head. You should get 320.

answer.html: sealed interface Rule permits Flat, Percent, AllOf {} record Flat(long minor) implements Rule {} record Percent(int bps) implements Rule {} record AllOf(List<Rule> rules) implements Rule { AllOf { rules = List.copyOf(rules); } // immutable: copy what the caller passed } static long fee(Rule r, long amountMinor) { return switch (r) { // no default: a new node type breaks the build case Flat f -> f.minor(); case Percent p -> amountMinor * p.bps() / 10_000; case AllOf a -> a.rules().stream().mapToLong(x -> fee(x, amountMinor)).sum(); }; }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: sealed interface Rule { data class Flat(val minor: Long) : Rule data class Percent(val bps: Int) : Rule class AllOf(rules: List<Rule>) : Rule { val rules: List<Rule> = rules.toList() // immutable: copy what the caller passed } } fun fee(r: Rule, amountMinor: Long): Long = when (r) { // no else: a new node type breaks the build is Rule.Flat -> r.minor is Rule.Percent -> amountMinor * r.bps / 10_000 is Rule.AllOf -> r.rules.sumOf { fee(it, amountMinor) } }

recap: Composite: single items and groups share one interface, and a group answers by asking its children. A sealed type plus an exhaustive switch or when replaces the GoF Component class.
Leave out default and else, and a new node type becomes a compile error at every operation that handles the tree.
Keep trees immutable with List.copyOf in a compact constructor (Java) or toList() (Kotlin), so they can be shared by many merchants and threads.
Bridge splits two dimensions that vary on their own, such as alert type and channel, so they cost N + M classes instead of N x M. You design it up front; an adapter is retrofitted.
Flyweight shares immutable instances: the Integer cache for -128 to 127, interned strings, Currency, enums. Build your own with a private constructor and computeIfAbsent, over a bounded set.
Never compare boxed numbers with == in Java. Kotlin's == calls equals.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why fee takes the payment amount as a parameter instead of storing it in the plan, and why that lets 40,000 merchants and 200 request threads share a dozen plan objects safely.
explain.answer: The plan holds only what is the same for every use: the rates, fixed fees and caps. That is its intrinsic state. The amount changes with every payment, so it is extrinsic state, and the caller passes it in. Because the plan never stores anything per payment, one plan object can serve every merchant on that plan. It is also immutable: record fields are final and the child lists are copied with List.copyOf. Once it's published safely, for example in a static final field built at startup, any number of threads can read it at the same time with no locks, because nothing ever writes to it. If the plan kept "the current amount" in a field, two threads pricing at once would overwrite each other, and you'd need one plan per merchant or a lock on every call.

deeper.html:
The GoF book spends pages on Composite's "transparency versus safety" choice: should add and remove live on the shared Component type, so leaves must throw, or only on groups, so callers must cast? A sealed type with immutable records ends the debate. There are no child-management methods at all: you build a new tree. Pattern matching gives each operation exact access to each node type, with no casts.

Recursion over a tree is fine for fee plans a few levels deep. A tree built from outside input (a rules engine fed by a merchant portal, say) could be thousands of levels deep and throw StackOverflowError. Validate the depth when you build the tree, or walk it with an explicit stack. Composite also pairs with Visitor; lesson 10 of this track, Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento, shows why sealed types and pattern matching usually replace it.

The Integer cache bounds are part of the contract: valueOf "will always cache values in the range -128 to 127, inclusive, and may cache other values outside of this range". The upper bound can be raised with the java.lang.Integer.IntegerCache.high system property. That can make a boxed == bug disappear on one JVM and show up on another, which is one more reason never to rely on it.

String interning has a GC cousin. G1's -XX:+UseStringDeduplication lets the collector make duplicate String objects share one backing array, with no code change. It saves memory for services that hold many equal strings (currency codes, country codes, status names) but doesn't make == work, because the String objects themselves stay distinct.
